https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/02.title: Just Stop Oil stunt 'made people care less about climate change'
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/02.subtitle: Green activists' behaviour ‘will do nothing but make us all colder and poorer’, people told survey
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2023/02.text:
Green protests in which activists blocked roads and threw soup over a Van Gogh artwork turned people off climate change action, a new survey has found.
The soup stunt by activists from the Just Stop Oil group, and roadblocks of the M25 by Insulate Britain had more than 50 per cent disapproval in a study of 3,000 people conducted last year by Opinium.
Both protests increased support for the view that “climate action will do nothing but make us all colder and poorer”, the survey found.
Roadblocks by Just Stop Oil were also found to be ineffective at winning people over, and left over-40s less willing to take action on climate change.
The roadblocks, which began in 2021, were met with anger by drivers and members of the public and prompted the Government to introduce new police powers to deter them.
Participants in the survey were split into groups and shown videos of five different climate protest actions, and their views compared to a control group who were not shown anything.
The most successful in boosting support for climate change action were protests by group Extinction Rebellion in 2019, and paint attacks on Government buildings by Just Stop Oil last year.
Both left participants more likely to say the Government should do more to combat climate change, and more willing to take action themselves.
The survey was commissioned by Steve Akehurst, a climate campaigner, who said the Van Gogh protest and Insulate Britain’s road blocks had “failed”.
Speculating on the reasons, he said “the first was a target that probably appeared random to most people; the second marred by scenes of dispute with ordinary members of the public.”
Earlier this year Extinction Rebellion said it would change its tactics away from roadblocks and public disruption to focus on more “collective” protest action.
“Because successful and influential stunts are genuinely hard to pull off, activists (understandably) occasionally fall-back on the idea that, basically, all publicity is good publicity,” said Mr Akehurst. “If there’s one thing this experiment proves, it’s that that this isn’t true.”

image.caption: Activists throwing soup over a Van Gogh painting turned people off climate change action

author: Emma Gatten

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/desti.title: The Cotswolds town that’s home to Extinction Rebellion and a vegan football club
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/desti.subtitle: With its reputation for ‘alternative’ lifestyles, left-field Stroud is like nowhere else in Britain
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/desti.text:
Much to my surprise, I’m dancing around the tables in a cafe while a Brazilian woman in a brown poncho and big beads shakes a maraca. The air smells of frankincense and chocolate. Another participant in this “cacao ceremony” is also wearing a poncho, but the rest of us wouldn’t raise an eyebrow in Waitrose. We all shed our woollies – and inhibitions – as the 100 per cent (fair-trade, organic) cocoa, ritual “smudging” and music venerating Pacha Mama, warm us up.
“Cacao ceremonies are the latest thing in the world of yoga and mindfulness,” says the bearded poncho man during a break. Stroud’s newest cafe, Coco Caravan, owned by chocolatier couple Jacques Cöp and Patricia Brien, opens to the public on Fridays and Saturdays – and for occasional events such as this £20, two-and-a-half hour ritual, an echo of traditional ceremonies held on auspicious occasions across Latin America.
Coco Caravan is one of many offbeat businesses – some new, some established – in Stroud, a corner of the Cotswolds like no other. Just outside the western limit of the AONB, Stroud has always been left field. The mostly red-brick town has had a predominantly Green council for about 20 years. Its reputation for “alternative” lifestyles dates back to “its history of nonconformism,” according to Tom Herbert, co-founder of The Long Table, which offers tasty meals on a “pay-what-you-can” basis in a Victorian riverside mill rescued from dereliction last year.
Decades ago, abandoned mills – Stroud is surrounded by five valleys – led to an influx of artists and creative types who set up homes and studios on the cheap. Damien Hirst has an art factory nearby. Today though it is Stroud’s environmentalists who make headlines. It is the birthplace of Extinction Rebellion and home to vegan football club Forest Green Rovers, owned by Dale Vince, founder of renewable energy company Ecotricity.
At The Long Table, I met local resident Penny and her friend Pippa, visiting to see what it was all about. Penny’s husband was there reluctantly. “I’m not that way inclined,” he said. “I just came because the boss wanted to,” he said, nodding in Penny’s direction. “We read the Daily Telegraph and Financial Times,” he said. “But if you want to see something odd, come to Stroud.” Penny then told me about a neighbouring community who didn’t believe in land ownership, “so they bought some land and then ritually ‘unbought’ it by tearing up the deeds.” They built their own homes. “You see them on the common every solstice, welcoming the sun,” she added.
“We’re changing the world one bite at a time,” said The Long Table’s Tom Herbert. “If we do food well we could change the world for the better.” He only buys ingredients from those farming “regeneratively”. That means “fewer chemicals and enhancing biodiversity,” he explained. “Working with nature rather than against it.”
You might be forgiven for thinking it all sounds like an episode of The Archers. After all, Stroud Farmers’ Market was the first to be mentioned on the BBC Radio 4 soap opera. (Fictitious) Ambridge isn’t far away.
Much of what is happening in Stroud revolves around food and drink, it seems. That Saturday market sees traders selling artisan breads, organic fruit, vegetables and more. One of the newest stalls, Slad Valley Mushrooms, sells lion’s mane, speckled chestnut and grey oyster varieties, all grown on waste sawdust. Nearby, Birch cafe was doing a brisk trade in oat milk flat whites as market shoppers, with wicker baskets of golden beets and organic cheeses, took a break.
Newer venues of interest to gourmands include Stroud Wine Company in pretty cobbled Withey’s Yard. Inside, owners Richard and Laura Holloway were preparing for an evening tasting session. The couple relocated from Sussex and opened in Stroud in 2017, adding a tasting room in 2021. “Coming from Sussex we were so pleased to find Woodchester Valley,” said Laura. The nearby vineyard has just won a Global Master’s Medal for its 2021 sauvignon blanc, which is now sold out.
Kendrick Street has arty independents and clothes stores such as Rasmachaz, a charity shop where the proceeds go to refugee projects in Calais. Over £50,000 has been donated so far. The shop’s creator, ‘Jeddi’, tells me how she spent her childhood living in a tiny fibreglass boat with her parents, three dogs and a parrot, cruising the nearby Gloucester & Sharpness Canal, sometimes venturing down the Severn Estuary. “We had to get rescued once,” she added.
Next stop was Stroud’s very fine museum, with its modern walled garden, where it was snowdrop weekend. “Stroud democratised galanthophilia,” said a man selling snowdrop bulbs for £80. In the 1950s, The Giant Snowdrop Company was the first in the UK to sell bulbs by mail order. “Until then it had just been a hobby for the landed gentry who swapped bulbs among themselves.”
In Stroud Valley Artspace, another example of social reform was underway. A couple of 20-somethings were smashing up a billiard table and making a noise with bass guitars. They had covered the gallery’s normally white walls and floor in painted paper, scribbled notes and scraps of material. Half-eaten food lay around. I seemed to be the only passer-by brave – or foolish? – enough to enter the gallery. Charlotte and Tom, otherwise known as Sunhead Kollektive, were coming to the end of a two-week youth residency. “It’s anti-art, anarchist, Dada-ist,” said Charlotte, with safety-pin ear-rings and orange hair. “Stroud is a bit cliquey, art-wise – a bit middle-class. We’re subverting that.”
I escaped their teen chaos and walked a pleasant two miles along the towpath towards my hotel. The canal is under restoration, bringing new life into the area. I saw otters, moorhens and kingfishers.
Canal-side, organic, solar-powered Stroud Brewery serves pizzas cooked in a wood-fired oven, and was busy with families at long wooden tables. After a tasty vegan pizza, I walked onwards, along the towpath, past Studio 18, a warehouse art space, and up a dark twisty lane to Burleigh Court Hotel, a quiet Georgian manor house three miles outside of Stroud. Its new owners spent £350,000 on a makeover. The rooms are a perfect retreat, its restaurant a wood-panelled, candle-lit haven. The food is also exquisite, with produce mostly sourced within a 35-mile radius, bee-hives in the grounds providing honey, and herbs growing in the kitchen garden.
Among my fellow diners were monied locals and Londoners exploring pretty Cotswolds villages. The Londoners visit the Cotswolds regularly, they said. “We usually take the train to Stroud and then get a taxi out immediately,” said one. “But it sounds like we should explore a bit. Not the cacao ceremony, though.”

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.title: Germans tell eco activists: ‘Stop glueing yourself to roads and we’ll back your causes’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.subtitle: Mayor of Hanover accused of ‘giving in to blackmail’ after striking deal with Letzte Generation to end disruptive protests
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.text:
The German city of Hanover has been accused of “giving in to blackmail” after it agreed to lobby for the demands of radical climate activists in return for them leaving the city in peace.
Manuel Hoeferlin, a senior figure in the governing Free Democrats, said that it was “naive and dangerous” for local municipalities to “give in to blackmail” by the climate activists, warning that this would only encourage them to “escalate” their tactics.
Last week, Belit Onay, the mayor of Hanover, confirmed that he had sent a letter to the heads of the parties represented in the German parliament, urging them to take up three central demands of the climate group Letzte Generation (Last Generation).
In return, the group, whose activists block traffic by glueing themselves to roads, said that it would “completely cease” its protests in the north German city.
The letter, signed by Mr Onay, called on the parties to bring in a speed limit of 100kph (62mph) an hour on the autobahn, subsidise a €9 (£8) rail ticket and set up “people’s assemblies” that would work out how to make the country carbon neutral by the end of the decade.
Mr Onay, who is also a member of the German Green Party, conceded that he had met the group for talks after their repeated blockades of the city’s streets had led to “extreme polarisation” among locals.
He denied that he had caved in to blackmail, saying that he shared Letzte Generation’s conviction that more needed to be done to cut carbon emissions.
“You only get blackmailed if you do something you don’t want to do,” he said, adding that the group’s demands were “all absolutely understandable.”
However, senior figures in several factions in the Bundestag have criticised the letter, saying that it will encourage that group to continue breaking the law until its demands are met.
Andrea Lindholz, a member of the conservative CSU party, said that: “Mr Onay and the Greens are supporting a movement that continuously and deliberately commits crimes in order to push their agenda.”
She told Die Welt newspaper: “Crimes are no more a part of achieving an objective than are threats of violence or extortion. I have no sympathy for that.”
Matthias Miersch, a member of the centre-Left Social Democratic Party, said that “politicians shouldn’t open themselves up to blackmail”.
Over the weekend, a spokesman for Letzte Generation called on other town mayors to follow suit.
Theodor Schnarr said: “Civil resistance has once again been crowned with success. We call on all mayors to start talks following the example of Hanover.”
Set up in late 2021, Letzte Generation has employed similar tactics to Just Stop Oil in the UK, with members glueing themselves to busy streets during rush hour, or trespassing onto airport runways.
While they initially focused the protests on Berlin, they have started blocking streets across the country in recent months.
The organisation targets road traffic due to what they see as the irresponsible emissions caused by people travelling to work by car.
Authorities have long complained that the illegal protests risk costing lives by slowing down the work of emergency services.
Last November, the group was widely condemned after a protest in Berlin held up a crane that was supposed to free a cyclist who had been caught under a lorry and who later died in hospital.

image.caption: Police remove Letzte Generation activists during a protest in Berlin in January
Belit Onay, the mayor of Hanover, said he shared Letzte Generation’s conviction that more needed to be done to cut carbon emissions

author: Jörg Luyken
